title: AI in Health Care Moves Toward More Autonomous Roles — The Monitor
key_facts: New federal pilot programs are testing AI tools that perform clinical functions usually done by physicians: talking to patients, giving therapy, diagnosing and recommending or adjusting treatment with less direct physician involvement.
According to The New York Times, more than 200 companies have CMS approval to test such tools, and the FDA has allowed four for Medicare patients outside its standard approval process.
Examples: a chatbot delivering cognitive behavioural therapy and a federally funded project to adjust heart-failure medication under physician oversight.
The AMA says AI should support, not replace, physicians; an August 2026 JAMA perspective argued AI could soon match or exceed physicians at several tasks.
FDA says newer uses may be harder to evaluate because outputs can be unpredictable and change over time; it has no rules yet and takes public comment until 19 October 2026.
A 2025 JAMA Health Forum letter found 60 of 950 FDA-cleared AI devices were recalled 182 times combined.
KFF polling (Sept 2025): 32% would trust a health app that uses AI to access their records.
quote_evidence: This marks a shift beyond AI’s more established role in narrower tasks, like reviewing scans or test results.
The agency has not yet established rules for evaluating this newer category of AI and is accepting public comment through October 19, 2026.
why_it_matters_hint: Federal pilots are moving AI towards doctor-like roles before evaluation rules exist.
event_date: KFF Monitor of 8 Oct 2026; underlying NYT report date not stated
notes: KFF relays The New York Times for the 200-company and four-FDA figures; NYT not opened. The newsletter also covers health misinformation topics not used here.
